analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical manufacturers to prove their products are safe for children, workers, and consumers before selling them.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 109th Congress ended with only three cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled the nation's main chemical safety law. Unlike drugs and pesticides, most industrial chemicals can be sold today with no federal toxicity review at all. The bill would have required every chemical maker to certify to the EPA that its product is safe — especially for fetuses, infants, and children — to fund biomonitoring to see which chemicals end up in people's blood, to ban chemicals that fail the safety test or that EPA never gets around to reviewing, and to publish the toxicity data in a public database.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, workers, and consumers generally, by shifting the burden of proving chemical safety from the public onto manufacturers. The bill set a goal of eliminating harmful chemical exposures by 2020 and required safety reviews of at least 300 of the riskiest chemicals first, plus biomonitoring studies and a public toxicity database so people could see what they are exposed to.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, manufacturers of most chemical substances are not required to supply any human or environmental toxicity information before selling their products; the bill's findings state the EPA has reviewed the health risks of only about 2 percent of the 62,000 chemicals in use when the law was written, and has banned or restricted only 5 substances in 29 years [S3].

Within one year, every chemical maker would have to submit a safety certification signed by its CEO, plus all toxicity data in its possession, and update it at least every three years or whenever new toxicity information emerged [S3].

EPA would rank the riskiest chemicals on a priority list of at least 300 substances — including those found in human blood, food, or drinking water — and decide within three years whether each meets a safety standard with an extra 10-fold protection factor for children; chemicals that fail, or that EPA cannot review in time, could no longer be sold [S3].

Manufacturers of chemicals produced in volumes over 1 million pounds a year would have to run biomonitoring studies to test whether the chemicals show up in human blood and tissue, and publish a method the public can use to detect them [S3].

The bill would create a public database of chemical toxicity and exposure information and clarify that chemical names and health effects can never be treated as trade secrets, while preserving states' right to adopt stricter rules [S3].
It would also fund research into animal-testing alternatives and a green chemistry program to reward development of safer substitute chemicals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, who would bear the cost of safety testing, certifications, biomonitoring studies, and possible loss of sales for chemicals that cannot be shown safe. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed through to consumers in product prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill shifts the burden of proof onto manufacturers: a chemical that cannot be shown to meet the safety standard — including any EPA has not reviewed by its deadline — cannot be sold [S3]. An honest supporter would acknowledge this could pull useful, low-risk products off the market while testing catches up, and that the bill authorizes substantial new spending (tens of millions of dollars a year for green chemistry centers alone) [S3].

The compliance burden falls hardest on smaller manufacturers, which is why the bill pairs it with technical-assistance centers, but testing and certification costs would still likely be passed on to consumers in prices [S3].

EPA would have to make safety determinations on tight statutory deadlines for thousands of substances; if the agency misses them, the bill's own mechanism automatically removes chemicals from commerce, which could create supply disruptions the President could only fix with case-by-case, renewable 5-year exemptions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes — reducing children's exposure to untested toxic chemicals — are large, and the bill's cost falls mainly on the industry creating the risk rather than on the public. The main honest concern is design risk: automatic sales bans when EPA misses deadlines could disrupt supply chains, and the transition would be expensive for manufacturers, with some of that cost passed to consumers. On balance the trade favored public health over industry convenience, which is precisely the trade the bill never got the chance to make.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Kid Safe Chemicals Act on November 10, 2005, joined by three Democratic cosponsors [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on December 2, 2005, to its Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

The bill's own findings documented why its sponsors thought it was needed: the EPA had reviewed the risks of only an estimated 2 percent of the 62,000 chemicals in use when the Toxic Substances Control Act passed in 1976, and had banned or restricted only 5 substances in 29 years because of the law's high legal hurdles [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided the testing, certification, biomonitoring, and potential sales bans the bill would have imposed, and the public never got the safety reviews or the toxicity database. Anyone exposed to industrial chemicals — that is, everyone — got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support; the Republican-run committee that controlled its fate never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required each manufacturer to certify its chemicals as safe before sale, submit all toxicity data, run biomonitoring studies, and lose the right to sell any chemical EPA could not clear — a fundamental reversal of the current rule that chemicals are presumed safe until proven harmful. Its interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the public's interest in knowing what chemicals it is exposed to.

Mandatory toxicity testing, biomonitoring studies, and periodic data audits would have created a large stream of paid testing work, with EPA randomly inspecting 3 percent of labs a year to keep the data reliable.

The bill would have created market incentives — expedited review, a marketing designation, public awards, and regional green chemistry research centers funded at $30-40 million a year — to reward substitutes for hazardous chemicals.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of consumer products made with chemicals
industries.note: Downstream product makers would face possible reformulation costs if an ingredient was banned, but would gain a public database showing which chemicals in their supply chains are hazardous, and could win market share by qualifying for the safer-alternative designation.
